utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I see that Mr. Gotovina and Mr. Markac have waived their right to be present in court today. Mr. Cermak, you are therefore alone now. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll try to deal with a couple of procedural matters so that we know what we still have to do during the recess period, or what we don't have to do anymore. I would first like to deal with scheduling issues after the recess. Not everything is yet entirely clear how we would use our time after the recess and for what exactly. Let me start with one informal recess that there would be a break between the conclusion of the Gotovina Defence case and the start of the Cermak Defence case. The Chamber, at this moment, on the basis of the reasons presented, has not decided to grant a seven- or ten-days' break, but more will become clear, perhaps if we deal with scheduling as a whole. What we know at this moment is that the Gotovina Defence intends to call five witnesses after the recess, the total number of hours scheduled for examination-in-chief being 21 hours. There still are a few uncertain matters, such as an application for 92 bis witnesses where no decision has yet been taken, where we do not even know what the position of the Prosecution will be, whether they want the Chamber to call the witnesses, the witness to be called for cross-examination. We further have - and I'll deal with that at a later stage - we have an expert report which is sought to be admitted through taking judicial notice of it, so there are still a few uncertain factors anyhow. Let's go back to the five witnesses after the recess. On the basis of the information the Chamber has received on the time needed for cross-examination, which is a little bit over 40 hours, this would result in total time for examination-in-chief and cross-examination of some 64 hours, which equals 18 court days. The Chamber recently has had the experience that sometimes the examination of witnesses took considerably less time than foreseen. Therefore, the Chamber invites the parties to see whether they can agree on a realistic schedule for the weeks after the break. That would mean starting 24th of August. So to come up with a realistic schedule which would take, at the maximum, 15 days for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. If it could be done in less than 15 days, the Chamber would certainly appreciate that. Apart from that, the Chamber urges the Gotovina Defence to organise the work in such a way that we would not have frequent gaps in which considerable court time is -- remains unused. The Chamber is aware that this may cause specific problems. When I think of Witness AG-2, I can imagine that that might not be easy. But, nevertheless, the Chamber invites the Gotovina Defence to use all its inventivity in order to avoid what has happened recently, that is, that we are not in court for considerable time. This would result, if agreed upon, at -- in finishing the Gotovina Defence case certainly not later than the 11th of September, and preferably earlier. As far as the start of the Cermak Defence case is concerned, the Chamber provisionally schedules the Cermak -- the start of the presentation of the Cermak Defence on the 17th of September. So despite the fact that the Chamber found no reasons to grant a break, the practical effect might be, depending on how matters develop, that there will be some break. At the same time, the Chamber has considered that, of course, the Cermak Defence should not be entirely dependant on, I would say, the behaviour of other parties, the Chamber, and, of course, the Cermak Defence itself, during the preceding weeks. The Chamber will, of course, first of all, have a close look at any agreed schedule the parties come up with, and the Chamber will further closely monitor what actually happens during those weeks, and, on the basis of those observations, if there's any need to adapt the 17th of September as the starting date, whether it could be earlier or later, we'll look at it during those weeks. This, as far as scheduling is concerned any -- I noticed, for example -- the Chamber noticed and is, of course, unaware of what could happen, but in relation to Witness AG- -- I think he was scheduled for eight hours. If we look at the statement we have received until now if that would be the subject matter covered by the examination-in-chief, the Chamber is not yet fully convinced that that would take up eight hours. But, again, it could be that other matters not yet in the statement would be part of it, so the Chamber is hesitant to say anything, but -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we should prepare as if it would take that long. The reason being that the statement is short because the witness refused to read his daily communications with his superiors, if I can put it that way. And, therefore, it may be necessary in court to show him physically since he is not willing to look at the reports to show them in court and then to ask him questions on the basis on what he wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As I said before, the Chamber was unaware of what might arise in viva voce testimony compared to the statement, and this exactly are the kind of issues to be discussed between the parties. I asked the parties to agree on a realistic schedule. Any other matter in relation to scheduling? Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assist the Court, because having been given the date, 17th of September, and appreciated the issues that the Court is looking at, my first two witnesses will be expert witnesses, and I have been able to receive this morning their translated reports. They were reports prepared in the Croatian language, and they have now been translated for me. I have been able to review those reports, and that has enabled me to make a more realistic assessment as to how long they will be in direct examination. Those witnesses will be considerably shorter than the estimates given in our schedule. I think General Feldi was put at six hours to my recollection. Having seen his report, seen what it covers, and how it narrows the issues for me, I'm of the view, having had a quick read through today, that I could be one session of an hour and a half. So the Court will see that a considerable effect will be on the duration of our time with our -- our witnesses being in a position of being better informed, as I am now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Kay. The Chamber is appreciative of focus on the most efficient use of court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The second witness, Mr. Kovacevic, exactly the same. Having received his report late last night, having reviewed it quickly, I can see again my time is going to be considerably lessened with him. And I will obviously - now have I read it in English - be able to make those kinds of tactical decisions which will help the Court's scheduling, and I give notice to all parties that those two witnesses will be considerably lesser than anticipated in our 65 ter (G) submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. The expression of our appreciation when you had dealt with Mr. Feldi is therefore now doubled, because Mr. Kovacevic is included now as well. Any other matter in relation to scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the other matters that the Prosecution had wished to raise will have some effect on scheduling. I don't know if you care to hear those now or take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was -- I think there are two -- for me, there are at least two issues, the one being the provisional position taken by the Prosecution in relation to the 92 bis statements. There were 11 of them. And another matter, but we might deal with that at a later stage, is the -- how to deal with the expert report of -- on political propaganda, the expert report by Mr. de la Brosse, I think. These are the two matters which seem to be related to scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: We also have the Prosecution's request regarding disclosures on all remaining experts, which, for the reasons I'll mention later, will have an effect on scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was announced that -- it is on my agenda that you would like to address these matters. As far as 11 bis, as 92 bis witnesses is concerned, could you already give an indication of the position of the Prosecution in relation to the need to call these witnesses for cross-examination of that we can really treat them as 92 bis witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position with respect to the 11 witnesses, first of all, we will be filing written objections to those submissions. However, we're very seriously considering and quite likely will propose to simply submit the arguments which we would make regarding each witness, as well as the evidence which we would present regarding the witnesses, simply to do that in the submission, and leave it in the Court's hands as to whether or not it is necessary under 90(H) to discharge our obligation by actually putting these matters to the witnesses since most of them will deal with credibility in any respect, but we're certainly amenable to the idea of simply leaving it in the Court's hands as to whether they should be called or not. One other matter with respect to that. Mr. President, we would like to reserve the right in connection these witnesses since most of them are being called to rebut the testimony of one particular witness, we've tried to get the personnel file of that particular witness from the government of Croatia. We've sent numerous RFAs and reminders, that has not been forthcoming. The only disclosure we have ever had with respect to this particular witness has come through documents from the Defence. So given how these matters get resolved, we would, if we get our hands on that, seek to submit that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the Gotovina Defence will wait until it has received the written filing and then take a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for the last portion, I think we would object if they had an interest in the witness's personnel file. He was their witness on direct, and it should have been tendered at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The point being that we couldn't get it by that time. We still haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, with all due respect if Mr. Russo can confirm that they asked for the personnel file before the witness testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: On that, I can't be positive, Mr. President, but I will certainly check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes matters come up, but the Chamber will consider whether -- what to do with that, once it has seen all the -- the submissions by both parties. As far as discussions on these kind of matters are concerned, during the recess, most of the Judges can be reached, if urgent matters are to be decided upon. At the same time, Judges, as all lawyers would like to enjoy some of their holidays as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On that optimistic note, Mr. President, I wanted to make an oral motion along the exact same lines as what we did last year at the break concerning the time for filing responses, and ask orally move that the same procedure as appears at transcript page 7204, beginning at line 2, apply now with respect to the time to file responses to any motions that are filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, we look up page 7204. If there could be agreement between the parties on these matters, then, of course, we'd like to hear from you. I move to my -- having dealt with scheduling issues, I'll move to the next item on my agenda. The Chamber would like to deliver its decision on admitting Exhibits D1540, D1541, D1542, D1544, D1545, D1546 D1551, D1552, and D1567. On the 30th of June of this year, the Gotovina Defence tendered the following documents: D1540 through D1546. The Prosecution objected to their admission. On the same day, the Chamber invited the parties to make written submissions on the admissibility of those documents, which are Official Notes taken by the Zadar-Knin crime police department in 1995. D1546 also contains a statement signed by an interviewee. All of this can be found between transcript pages 19478 and 19503. On the 1st of July, the Gotovina Defence further tendered D1551 and D1552, which the Chamber included in its previous invitation to make written submissions. This can be found at pages 19596 and 19597. On the 2nd of July, 2009, D1567 was similarly tendered and added to the invitation. This can be found at transcript page 19716. On the 3rd of July, 2009, both the Prosecution and the Gotovina Defence filed their submissions. The Prosecution no longer objected to the admission of documents D1542 and D1546. The parties did not address D1551 and D1552 in their submissions. In its submissions, the Prosecution objected to the admission of the documents into evidence because they are statements of witnesses on the Gotovina Defence's witness list, and the Prosecution was informed that the Gotovina Defence no longer intended to call those witnesses to testify. The Prosecution submitted that the Gotovina Defence, by tendering those documents into evidence, was circumventing its decision not to call the witnesses, making reference to an oral decision the Chamber rendered on the 19th of November, 2008. That decision ordered the redaction of two paragraphs in William Hayden's statements that referred to the evidence of Colonel Hjertnes. In that particular case, the Chamber found it inappropriate to admit those portions into evidence. The present case differs in two significant respects. Firstly, the redacted statements were obtained for the purpose of judicial proceedings before this Tribunal, while the tendered documents are contemporaneous out of court statements prepared by non-parties and not taken for the purpose of the Tribunal's proceedings. Secondly, in the previous instances, there had been a dispute amongst the parties about whether Colonel Hjertnes, who made the later redacted statements, should be withdrawn. On the 10th of March, 2008, despite objections of the Gotovina Defence, the Chamber allowed the Prosecution to remove Colonel Hjertnes from the witness list. It was in light of this dispute that the Chamber found it inappropriate to include portions of documents which referred to Colonel Hjertnes's withdrawn evidence. The Chamber did not make a general finding according to which the withdrawal of a witness from a witness list would preclude the admission into evidence of documents referring to the withdrawn evidence. In here relevant respect, the Chamber finds little merit in the analogy with the 19th of November 2008 decision as proposed by the Prosecution. The Chamber notes that it has previously admitted several Official Notes. In its 30th January 2009 decision, the Chamber determined that Official Notes may be admitted if they meet the requirements of Rule 89(C) and (D). That is, if the documents are relevant and of probative value, and the probative value is not substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. In the present case, no argument was advanced by the Prosecution challenging either the relevance or the probative value of the documents. The Gotovina Defence explained that it tendered the documents to show investigative steps taken by the Croatian civilian authorities with regard to incidents of killing, burning, and looting after Operation Storm. On the basis of this argument, and having examined the documents, the Chamber is satisfied that these contemporaneous official Croatian MUP documents satisfy the requirements for admission under Rules 89(C) and (D) of the Rules. The Chamber, therefore, admits into evidence D1540, D1541, 42, 44, 45, 46, D1551, 52, and D1567. The Chamber emphasises that the admission into evidence of these documents is in no way an indication of the weight, if any, which the Chamber may ultimately attach to them. And this concludes the Chamber's decision to admit the aforementioned documents into evidence. For the next item, we briefly have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber lifts the confidentiality of the Trial Chamber's decision on motion for provision release. This decision is dated the 2nd of December 2008 and concerns Mr. Cermak. I move to the next item on my agenda. The Gotovina Defence wanted to rely on 1D588, which is the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in Stanisic and Simatovic. That is what we understood that the Gotovina Defence wanted to do, and we will see what formal follow up should be given to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, if I could just make one correction, that 1D588 is the full pre-trial brief in agreement with the Prosecution. We have redacted portions of that brief to make it as relevant as possible to this case, and the redacted the version of that brief is now 1D2782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you have discussed the matter. You want to tender this into evidence. In view of the fact that you have discussed the matters with the Prosecution, does that mean that there's no objection or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We don't object to those portions of the Prosecution's -- the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in that case to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber wondered, in view of the fact that there is no objection to it, that to admit into evidence the parts of a pre-trial brief, of course, raises the issue what exactly the parties were seeking with that. And I think it's clear that the Gotovina Defence sought those portions to be in evidence, in order to have the Chamber look at the consistency of the positions taken by the Prosecution in the Stanisic/Simatovic case and the present case. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- the way things transpired is we proposed those portions to be stipulated as agreed facts between the parties. The Prosecution has, for its own reasons, asked that it not be done as a stipulation of agreed facts but that we tender it into evidence in the form that we are now tendering it into evidence. I would leave it my colleagues on the Prosecution side if there is any further issue regarding the form to address the matter. But from our perspective, we first wanted it as stipulation of agreed facts. And in discussions with our colleagues on the other side of the isle, we have agreed to accommodate them by tendering it in this form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it went further, it went to the truth of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apparently there is no agreement on the truth of the content such that could be submitted to this Chamber as agreed facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would leave it the Prosecution to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think -- I think, Mr. President, that the Chamber can appreciate the situation that these are allegations that the Prosecution has made in another case that it intends to prove in that case, and we were just uncomfortable with, at this stage, having one Chamber essentially agree to those facts and say that these, in fact, occurred, when these are the subject of another case where we will be seeking to prove those facts, and that's why -- of course, we don't -- those are facts we intend to prove in another case so we don't disagree with them, but, procedurally speaking, it seemed to be a bit of a strange situation. And that's why we propose to have it this way, so that at least it is clear that these are allegations that the Prosecution intends to prove in that case, but this is what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say if you would fail to offer sufficient evidence of those facts, that would you reconsider your position as to whether these are true facts or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no disagreement, from what I understand, that those portions were presented as the position of the Prosecution in that other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, indeed. And just the last issue on the -- on the stipulation was that when we were approached to stipulate to those facts, the reason also is, if you remember, we have raised a few relevance objections to it, so we did not want to be the proponents of the fact. That's why we propose that the Defence tenders them, and we will not object based on the Chamber's guidance and rulings we have received previously about matter that we believe are, at best, only peripherally relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic, any further -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please assign a number to 1D278.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1D2782. I'm always a bit puzzled because I thought that numbers would always have the same number of digits and -- but perhaps in 1D588, a zero is missing after the D. It's not. So they have -- if everyone understands, we're talking about ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm advised that it does not have to, Mr. President. Have four digits, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. We are talking, whatever the number is, about portions of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief in the Stanisic and Simatovic case. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's 65 ter 1D2782, and it becomes Exhibit D1625.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The Chamber appreciates the explanation the parties have given on how they -- from what angle they consider this exhibit. I would again like to go into private session for some moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Prosecution has indicated that it would like to address the issue of Defence disclosure obligations in relation to expert witnesses. Mr. Russo, is it you who will address the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, let me -- this is a rather lengthy history. I will try to cut it down. Basically what the Prosecution is looking for from the Defence is -- are three things at this point. We asked for more in the past, but we sort of whittled our interest down to three main things. Number one, a list of all of the information; that includes evidence, documents, or any other kind of information provided to each witness. Secondly, being any communications or all communications had between the Defence and their expert witnesses. And, thirdly, the draft -- any draft reports submitted by the experts to the Defence teams or vice versa as we heard in regard to the witness yesterday. Now, Mr. President, we fully understand the Defence`s position that there is no particular rule under which this material was requested. However, the basis for our request is simply that this -- and I believe we included this on the e-mail that was forwarded to Chambers, these are proper matters for cross-examination. The material that the witness reviewed, what they were told by the Defence, what they said to the Defence, any previous positions or changes they may have made in their reports, all proper areas for investigation on the cross-examination. We're simply trying to cut down the amount of time we have to spend with the witnesses on the stand, pulling this information out of them, when, if it is provided to us in advance, to could very easily become a non-issue for us. I can go through the history of our request for this, but suffice it to say that we asked for this material on the 6th of May, and then a follow-up, bit of a broader request on 7th of May, and we've been back and forth on the issue as the Court has seen through correspondence since then. We were provided with correspondence between the Gotovina Defence and Witness Cross, prior to his arrival on the stand which we were certainly appreciative of. Of course, we didn't get everything we asked for, but we understood that to mean that there would be such disclosures with regard to other witnesses. We couldn't get a definite answer on that. We did also have some discussions the other day with respect to Professor Corn's information, and we were told that we might receive a list of exhibits that will be used with him during cross-examination, and advisement as to whether that -- I'm sorry. On direct examination, an advisement as to whether that list encompasses what was shown to him prior to or whether it does not. However we would much prefer simply a transparent list for each witness of the documents or information given to them in order for them to prepare the reports or subsequently to that. The issue of draft reports and communications is attendant also for the same considerations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what I did some time ago is invite Mr. Russo to put his position in writing. We have fulfilled our obligations under Rule 97 concerning what we had to turn over to them. It is interesting to -- 67 excuse me, under Rule 67. It is interesting to note somewhat of an inconsistent position taken by the Prosecution on the disclosure of expert materials. Nevertheless there is a different obligation on the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would invite to you slow down. You wouldn't mind, would you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Mr. President. Sorry to the translators. There is clearly different disclosure obligations on the Prosecution under Rule 66 and 68, as opposed to what the disclosure obligations by the Defence under Rule 67. That being said, we invited the Prosecution to lay out their concerns and their legal basis for their request. And we would answer that request, and we invite them to do that once again. This is circumscribed by the rules. I hasten to add that Mr. Russo, himself, when we invited or asked the Court in the interest of justice to tell Mr. Russo to put his case concerning shelling to Mr. Rajcic, Mr. Russo said that Rule 90(H) only applies to cross-examination and not to direct examination. And as a result of that Rule, there was no basis upon which for him to require the Prosecution to put his case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask to you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies again. The answer to this, is quite simple. It falls within the four corners of Rule 67. We have complied with the Rule 67, and we will continue to comply with Rule 67. And we welcome the opportunity to answer any submission given to the Court by the Prosecution on this score. And again, my apologies to the interpreters for speaking so quickly. If I might have one moment. I'm reminded of one last fact by my colleague Mr. Misetic. And than is the position of the Prosecution today, in this case and others, is that they have no obligation to disclose communications with their witnesses, be it experts or otherwise. So given these positions, and given the inconsistent approach taken by the Prosecution in this case, we invited the Prosecution to make a submission to the Court, cite the legal basis upon which they request this information, and allow the Defence the appropriate time to respond as we, of course, will. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. First of all, regarding the allegation of an inconsistent position, I want to be clear, with respect to Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, I did provide the draft reports in advance of the witness coming. I did provide and in fact file with the addendum the list of material given to Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, and I did provide all communications we had with Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. So there is no inconsistency in that position. I'm not sure what the Rajcic 90(H) issue relates to, so I will simply pass that up. But with respect to any obligations, I have already made clear that we're not stating that this is an absolute obligation on the part of Defence under a particular rule to provide us with this information. We're asking for it in the interests of judicial economy. And if you want to basis, I can say Article 20 requires a fair and expeditious proceeding, but I don't think it is necessary to go that far. I think this is simply a matter of attempting to save time for both the Defence and the Court and all others concerned. But beyond that, Mr. President, since we were asking for this material for quite a lot of time and were not getting what we asked for, we simply went or attempted to go directly to the witnesses. I spoke to General Cross. I agreed to give me what I asked for. And he did in fact provide me with a PowerPoint presentation upon which he used -- based his initial report. But he a discussion with the Defence notice meantime, and they told him that - this is what he told me - that they would take care of the disclosure. So we attempted to get it directly from the witness, which I believe we're entitled to do. But if the Defence chooses to intervene and take responsibility for the disclosure, then I believe they do have some obligation to do it, or at least not attempt to interfere with us getting it directly from the witness. But that being said, Mr. President, I did put this position in writing as the Court can see from the e-mail which was forwarded to Chambers. I told Mr. Kehoe that our position was that this was material which is the proper subject of cross-examination and we were seeking this material for purposes of judicial economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Brief response, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Very brief. The response to General Cross as to every witness is that the disclosures would be made pursuant to the Rules. Quite simply that. That was fertile area for cross-examination by Mr. Hedaraly, as well it should have been. That doesn't, doesn't circumvent the Rule in which sets out the Defence's required disclosures under Rule 67. Now, with regard to the documents that are going to be used, we are going to give them and have given with regard to -- well, certainly cross and Corn, all of the documents that could be potentially used with Professor Corn. That includes those he looked in to rely on and those that he just examined and didn't rely on. Which, frankly, are fertile areas for cross-examination by the Prosecution. Now my reference to the Rule 94(H) was simply this: The Rule is the Rule. When the Prosecution saw fit to rely on the rules to get what they wanted, they responded that Rule 94(H) didn't require them to cross during their direct case. We are simply asking the Chamber to comply with the Rules, and we will disclose our obligations under Rule 67, and it's simple as that. My analogy to Rule 94 was nothing more than that. Excuse me, Rule 90(H) was nothing more than that. And that's the simple response, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Of course, a reference to simplicity always triggers -- if matter are as simple as that, one would wonder why Mr. Russo doesn't see that. Is there any of the other parties who would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an issue that in our submission covers all of the interests of the Defence parties. It has arisen in the Gotovina case, and the issues have been discussed between the Prosecution and counsel for General Gotovina. But, of course, there are repercussions for the remaining Defence teams. Your Honour, the issue in our submission was very clearly set out by the Prosecution team themselves in their filing on the 18th of November, 2008. The Prosecution response to the Gotovina Defence motion to compel the disclosure of draft expert report of Reynaud Theunens. It's perhaps interesting to recollect how this issue arose. Mr. Theunens was interviewed by the Gotovina Defence team prior to his giving evidence. He revealed, because the trial for this case was originally scheduled at a much earlier date, that he had presented a report to the Prosecution very few weeks before the original trial date of this case. They asked him if they could see that report, and he was willing to disclose it to them. This case was then put back, and we know that the Theunens expert report was filed on a later date, and that report contained significant changes, so far as we were concerned, in relation to his expertise concerning the position, role, and involvement of Mr. Cermak in this case. For my part, I had made no applications for Theunens's disclosures of drafts. Any matters that I would have dealt with would have been in cross-examination. So what arose did not come about as a result of anything said by me. When this issue was discussed in open court, Your Honour was aware of issues concerning legal professional privilege, that was documented in the transcript. Your Honour was aware of other issues that there had been no decision on this matter within the Tribunal jurisprudence, and both parties agreed on that. And then the matter was left at that. And Mr. Theunens was asked by Your Honour, and he voluntarily said that he would deliver that draft, and in fact it turned out there were three, four, or five versions, and they were disclosed to the Defence by Mr. Russo. The position, as I saw it then, having then seen the content of Mr. Theunens's draft, that this material fell fairly and squarely within Rule 68. It was material that was exculpatory; it was material that contradicted the Prosecution case, capable even going to mitigation of guilt, whatever expression it was. And, of course, this witness was an employee of the Prosecution, used as an expert, and of particular interest to the Defence, as a result of his relationship with his employers. So there it was. In the filing by the Prosecution that was made and in all their arguments, they made clear that their position was that they were only obliged to disclose materials within the Rules, and it was stated that, in paragraph 10 of the filing of the 18th of November, that having reviewed their materials, they said that there was nothing to trigger disclosure obligations under Rule 68. There are no such circumstances here. Well, in the outcome of the event, we were very concerned, because we disagree with that, and the impact of Mr. Theunens's statements which were dealt with in cross-examination, we submit clearly went to the issues within Rule 68. Our submission is, on this matter, that, in terms of documents considered by an expert, taking our example, our experts have -- have been given free range to look at any document they want within the database, within the materials of the Prosecution, Defence, anything. And we haven't constrained them. They have been allowed to work on their own in an office and look at materials, and, so, for my part, I couldn't tell you what they'd looked at because it is simply endless. If you make a position with Mr. Theunens, there has been no disclosure to us of what he looked at. Your Honour will remember the description of his task to me that he was considering documents, and they popped up on the screen or they didn't pop up on the screen. I just use that as an expression, because this is the reality of how it works, and how people inform themselves and brief themselves as to what they see and how they construct a report. In relation to communications, well these are plainly covered by legal professional privilege. I have no reason to hide behind that, but I'm making this as a stand because this is an important principle of law litigated in this Tribunal in the very first case of Tadic concerning the impact of legal professional privilege, and it is a matter upon which the whole structure of legal systems are built. And I'm not going to be the advocate who starts conceding on such a matter. In relation to drafts and opinions, a draft can exist probably 100 times a day. Any change you make to a document means that a document is moved from one state to another. In our submission, that is, in these technological days, something impossible to capture. The issue on Theunens, however, was because he had submitted a report as an expert, and that was what the Gotovina team were particularly interested in. It was given a title, a draft. I don't know whether it was meant to be a -- a preliminary report, a report at all, or a draft. That was just how that played out. Sometimes in litigation that is what happens. But in our submission, there is no requirement for the Defence to supply the Prosecution with drafts. They must do their job by cross-examination of a witness, ask him if he has always consistently held a point of view. If he says yes, investigate. If he says, no, well, where was your previous point of view? These are matters of cross-examination rather than disclosure, and, in our submission, we do no more than is necessary under our disclosure obligations within the Rules, which strive to comply with. And that's what we submit is the proper basis for litigation between the parties. Your Honour, those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Anything the Markac Defence would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In order to be being repetitive as my learned friend before me stressed the situation, I would only quote my learned friend Mr. Russo from the OTP, page 21, line 20: "There is no particular rule under which the requested material should be presented to the Office of the Prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If could I just make one point for the record, Mr. President. Mr. Russo stated that we had interfered in some communication he had with Witness Cross. We received an e-mail communication between Witness Cross and Mr. Russo. As far as I know, the documents that Mr. Cross indicated would be provided to Mr. Russo were provided to him, and if they weren't, we weren't subsequently told by Mr. Russo that there was something in addition that was missing from whatever his agreement was with Mr. Cross. I just wanted to be clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether it will ask for further written submissions on the matter. This may, however, be clear that there are several elements involved in this discussion. One is, and that's the one that has been stressed at least this morning very much by Mr. Kehoe, is disclosure obligations. There are, however, other aspects as well, such as for a Chamber to evaluate the probative value of an expert report, and I think we can find this in the case law of this Tribunal as well, it is important to know what sources were used by that expert, what methodology he applied. So, therefore, apart from whether there is any disclosure obligation, let's just, for argument's sake, assume, which I think has not happened until now, that it would be unclear what sources were given to or were used, whether they popped up or not on the screen of the expert, then, of course, it would be very difficult to assess to what extent the special skills, the special expertise of the expert would have been properly applied on relevant, factual material. Now, what we've seen in the past is that -- let me add a third issue. That is, the genesis of a report I think everyone would agree with Mr. Kay that what is a draft, of course, it changes every minute not only in expert reports but even drafts for decisions. At the same time there comes a moment when the content of the draft is shared with another person, another draft, which opens possibilities for exchanges, which can - I emphasise the word "can" - have an influence on the next draft. Therefore -- and that's different for all of the expert reports. The genesis of those reports have sometimes triggered full attention, whereas in other circumstances, no one seemed to be very much interested in it, whether the expert is working on his desk, see what pops up on his screen, or whether he has a discussion with members of a team of a party who then provide a first draft based on those conversations, might be an element which could have some importance in evaluating. So we've seen that apart from the disclosure obligations, there's more involved. That is, the understanding, full understanding, and there, of course, is a difference between a witness and an expert, a full understanding as to how these opinions came into being on the basis of what facts provided, on the basis of what -- on the basis of what series of documents being made available, or we do not know, then -- at least we could ask the expert whether he used them all or whether he stopped halfway or -- these are important matters not only from a point of view of disclosure but also important matters in view much evaluation, evidentiary evaluation of the expert report. Finally, there's a third element; that is, judicial economy. That is, if you have not available to yourself already some of the relevant data, it might take quite a bit of time in court to explore these matters with, as a possible result, that finally, they turned out not to be relevant. Mr. Kay very much emphasised the importance of cross-examination. These are the three elements. That is, disclosure; second, the proper evaluation of what the expert report brings us; and the third is judicial economy. We're not going at this moment, of course, to decide on the matter. What I will discuss with my colleagues is whether we think that we have received sufficient information on this issue, that sufficient argument has been raised, or whether we would give an opportunity to -- or even ask the parties to make written submissions on the matter. We'll have a break, although I was confident that we might do in one session, we'll certainly conclude in the next session. We will have a break, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

The Chamber is not asking the parties to do so, which would not prevent them, perhaps, from making further submissions, but we're not inviting the parties. If, however, a party would like to make further submissions, then we'd like to receive them in two days -- in one week from today, so that it doesn't come at the end. Further, Mr. Kay, you have referred to professional secrecy in the Tadic case. Well, I'm not pretending any ignorance on what may have happened in that case. utterances.text: I think that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So we had no objection, and I think Mr. Russo advised Chambers that we had no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the speakers to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were advised that there were no objections which means that P2585 is ready to be admitted and is admitted into evidence. Then the last one on my list is -- are related to Stjepan Sterc. We'll deal with that at a later stage. Also -- let me see. Yes, we'll not deal with them at this very moment. This concludes then we have at least been able to shorten the MFI list considerably. Any other matter to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's one matter concerning the Rule 68 motion filed by the Cermak Defence, I think at the end of May, Your Honour. This also has an impact on the scheduling for the case, because of the work required on our part to analyse and present materials to enable the issues in the case that we seek to rely upon to be put before the Trial Chamber using Rule 92 bis. We have been able to conduct some of these analyses already from materials we've had access to and that are publicly available. Those relevant witnesses form a considerable part of our Rule 65 ter (G) filing as to our witnesses, but that is in terms of quantum rather than court time, as the Court appreciates the use of the 92 bis system for corroborative evidence and the related provisions. I'm conscious that I have a case that will be, say, two months, eight weeks, seven weeks, eight weeks, and when I come to close the Cermak Defence case, it has been my intention to use the last day as the 92 bis day when all the relevant procedural requirements are performed in court, so that we have our live evidence first, and then the structure, as I see it, is best served by having the 92 bis evidence right at the end. And I'm doing it for that reason because I'm conscious that there may be further disclosure to us, as there has been thus far. And such projects, I know, take a considerable amount of resources and time, and I've had to make financial provision to ensure that and hire a new member of staff to take that particular task on from within -- to assist my team. I don't want to be in the position, when concluded my case, of saying to the Court, I'm sorry, we just have not had time to review this material and make an appropriate filing. I think that that would be unsatisfactory, probably. So I -- I do flag this up before the Court, as something that members of my team who are dealing with this, have constantly raised with me, and I'm a little bit concerned now as we're getting ever closer to the start of our Defence case, and I want to make sure that we have everything in proper place for our window of opportunity to present our evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is therefore mainly to inform the Chamber about what you're doing at this moment rather than to require the Chamber to take any action at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We're looking to the Chamber for a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in a, I hope, gentle way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would appreciate if you didn't have to wait too long. Isn't that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, yes, and Your Honours' colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter? There being nothing on the agenda anymore, we will adjourn, but I would first wish to everyone in this courtroom that they will have -- and I know how difficult it is sometimes to relax during this holiday time. I'm also aware that those who are in detention, even if not here, of course, it is different for them, especially those who have to stay here. Nevertheless, I wish everyone a good four weeks to come, three weeks of recess and one week of not sitting. And we resume on Monday, the 24th of August, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of August, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 25

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
